segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that time the disciples came to Jesus and asked,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who, then, is greatest in the kingdom of the heavens?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He called a child over, set the child in their midst,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble—it would be better for him to have a donkey millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks! For stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the person through whom the stumbling block comes!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than to have two hands or two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the Gehenna of fire.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: See that you do not look down on one of these little ones, for I tell you that their angels in the heavens always see the face of my Father in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go and search for the one that is straying?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if he manages to find it, truly I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that never went astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way, it is not the will of your Father in the heavens that one of these little ones should be lost.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If your brother sins against you, go and point out his fault, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if he does not listen, take one or two others along with you, so that ‘every matter may be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly; and if he refuses to listen even to the assembly, let him be to you like a Gentile and a tax collector.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again, truly I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about any matter they ask for, it will be done for them by my Father in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Peter came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, how many times shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason the kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a king who wanted to settle accounts with his slaves.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When he began the settling, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Since he had no means to repay, the master ordered him to be sold, along with his wife and children and everything he had, and the debt to be repaid.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So the slave fell to the ground and bowed down before him, saying, ‘Be patient with me, and I will repay you everything.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Moved with compassion, the master of that slave released him and forgave him the loan.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But that slave went out and found one of his fellow slaves who owed him a hundred denarii, and he seized him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay back what you owe.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So his fellow slave fell down and begged him, saying, ‘Be patient with me, and I will repay you.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But he refused. Instead he went and threw him into prison until he should repay what was owed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When his fellow slaves saw what had happened, they were deeply distressed, and they went and reported to their master everything that had happened.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then his master summoned him and said to him, ‘You wicked slave! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And in his anger his master handed him over to the torturers until he should repay all that was owed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts.”

notes.note: Matthew's Greek has the plural, “the heavens,” which reflects Hebrew and Aramaic idiom and would have sounded Semitic to a Greek ear. Most English translations flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here wherever the Greek has it; the singular in verse 18 is likewise the Greek's own.

notes.phrase: causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble
notes.note: The verb means to trip someone up so that they fall in their loyalty to God, whether into sin or out of faith. The older “offend” now suggests hurt feelings, and “cause to sin,” used by some modern versions, is narrower than the Greek. The related noun in verse 7 is rendered “stumbling block.”

Households ground grain with small hand mills; the “donkey millstone” was the large upper stone of a mill turned by an animal. Most translations say “a great millstone” or “a heavy millstone,” which gives the point but not the picture.

notes.traditional: hell fire; the hell of fire
notes.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which in Jewish usage had become the name for the place of final judgment. Many translations render it “hell,” which merges it with Hades and with later imagery. The name is kept here, as in several modern versions.

notes.phrase: the face of my Father in the heavens
notes.note: Verse 11 (“For the Son of Man came to save what was lost”) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not in the Greek text translated here. It was most likely added by copyists from Luke 19:10, and most modern translations omit it or place it in a footnote.

Some of the earliest manuscripts lack “against you,” so that the saying concerns any sin by a fellow believer and not only a personal wrong. The words may have been added under the influence of verse 21, or dropped by accident. Editors are divided, and the Greek text followed here includes them.

“Brother” here is not a sibling but a fellow member of the community of disciples, as the appeal to “the assembly” in verse 17 shows. The term covered women as well as men, and some translations render it “brother or sister” or “member of the church.”

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is recognizable everywhere.

The Greek construction can also be read “will have been bound in heaven,” so that the community's decision follows heaven's rather than the reverse; scholars disagree on how much weight the tense will bear. “Binding” and “loosing” are widely understood from Jewish usage as forbidding and permitting, and here, in a context of discipline, perhaps also as excluding and readmitting. The “you” is plural, where the same words in 16:19 are addressed to Peter alone.

The Greek can mean either “seventy-seven times” or “seventy times seven,” and translations are divided. The identical phrase appears in the Greek version of Genesis 4:24, where it stands for the Hebrew “seventy-sevenfold” of Lamech's boast of vengeance, and Jesus is probably echoing and reversing that boast. On either reading the point is forgiveness that does not keep count.

The Greek word denotes a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. The story depends on this: the master can order the man and his family sold. A king's slaves could hold high office and handle great sums, which explains the size of the debt. Most older translations, and several modern ones, have “servants.”

A talent was the largest unit of money, worth roughly six thousand denarii, and a denarius was about a day's wage for a laborer. Ten thousand was the highest number for which Greek had a single word, so the sum is deliberately beyond any possibility of repayment. The hundred denarii of verse 28 is a real but ordinary debt, about one six-hundred-thousandth of the first.

The Greek verb names prostration in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. Here a slave prostrates himself before his master to plead for time, so the physical gesture is rendered and not “worship,” as in the King James Version. Most modern translations do the same in this verse.
